p: One of the big stars here is the Staffordshire Hoard, the largest hoard of Anglo-Saxon gold and silver metalwork ever found. It was discovered by a metal detectorist in a Staffordshire field in 2009, and it's shared between this museum and the Potteries Museum in Stoke-on-Trent. Seeing that intricate gold work up close is a proper goosebumps moment.

The Pre-Raphaelite collection has a strong local link too. Edward Burne-Jones, one of the movement's big names, was born in Birmingham, and the museum holds a superb collection of his work alongside his fellow artists. If you love rich colours and storytelling paintings, give yourself time here.

The museum building opened in 1885, paid for in part by the profits of the city's gas department, which tells you a lot about Victorian Birmingham's ambitions. Parts of the museum have been closed in recent years for major building works, so it's worth checking which galleries are open before you set out. Allow a couple of hours for a good look round.

You're right in the civic heart of the city, so there's loads around you. Victoria Square, with the Council House, the Town Hall and the fountain locals know as the Floozie in the Jacuzzi, is just outside. Head the other way to Centenary Square and the Library of Birmingham, whose rooftop garden gives great views. The Jewellery Quarter is a short walk or tram ride away, and families can carry on to Thinktank science museum at Millennium Point. Birmingham New Street and Moor Street stations are both within walking distance.
